# **Architecting a Winning Academic Whitepaper for the Kaggle Gemma 4 Developer Agent Paper Track**

## **Foundational Principles of Academic Whitepapers in Machine Learning**

An academic whitepaper in computer science and machine learning occupies a distinct epistemological category that separates it from both industrial marketing collateral and standard competition solution logs1. Whereas a traditional competition post-mortem focuses on cataloging the sequence of heuristics that maximized a single scalar leaderboard metric, an academic whitepaper is an instrument of verifiable scientific communication2. Its primary objective is to isolate a fundamental computational bottleneck, formulate a falsifiable hypothesis regarding its resolution, and demonstrate through controlled empirical ablation why a specific architectural or algorithmic intervention succeeds or fails2. In the context of Google DeepMind's Gemma 4 Developer Agent Paper Track on Kaggle, this distinction is the primary determinant of success: achieving a high patch-resolution score on the leaderboard does not by itself satisfy the judging rubric, whereas a methodologically rigorous investigation of a baseline model's failure modes can contend for top honors even with a modest raw benchmark score2.  
The foundational architecture of a peer-reviewed whitepaper rests on four scientific pillars: problem formalization, variable isolation, external validity, and independent reproducibility1. Problem formalization requires moving beyond symptom description to identify the underlying mathematical or systems constraint—such as how quadratic self-attention scaling (![][image1]) and context window saturation degrade local model performance during multi-turn repository traversal4. Variable isolation demands that researchers establish a frozen, credible baseline and alter exactly one mechanism at a time while holding the base model weights, task splits, token budgets, and hardware allowances strictly constant2. When multiple hyperparameters, prompt rules, and retrieval tools are modified simultaneously, causal attribution becomes impossible, reducing the manuscript from a scientific study to an anecdotal engineering log2.  
Furthermore, a persuasive whitepaper prioritizes negative results and boundary conditions alongside positive performance gains2. In peer-reviewed venues such as NeurIPS—where top submissions from the Gemma 4 Paper Track will be showcased at a Google-hosted expo—reviewers actively penalize papers that claim universal superiority without documenting where the method breaks down1. Incorporating explicit ablation studies, such as removing graph edges from a code-graph retrieval system to test whether structural topology provides value beyond merely retrieving additional text tokens, proves that the proposed mechanism is the true driver of empirical improvement2. Finally, industrial research whitepapers must bridge theoretical elegance with deployment pragmatism, providing complete run-log schemas, deterministic verification scripts, and transparent resource accounting so that independent practitioners can replicate the findings with a single execution command2.

## **Competition Mechanics and Strategic Landscape of the Gemma 4 Paper Track**

The Gemma 4 Developer Agent initiative is bifurcated into two separate Kaggle competitions hosted by Google DeepMind: the main featured prediction competition (gemma-4-developer-agent) and the independent research paper track (gemma-4-developer-agent-paper)1. Understanding the structural divergence between these two tracks is essential for resource allocation and submission planning2. While the main competition evaluates automated code-fixing archives (submission.zip containing agent.yaml at its root) across approximately 120 hidden SWE-bench-style Python tasks until December 2, 2026, the Paper Track is a human-judged research competition that closes nearly three weeks earlier on Thursday, November 12, 2026, at 23:59 UTC2.  
Crucially, participation in one competition does not register a team for the other, nor is a main-track leaderboard entry required to compete in the Paper Track2. Analysis of participation metrics reveals a striking strategic asymmetry: while the main prediction competition has attracted approximately 3,891 teams competing for \$65,000 across three leaderboard ranks, the Paper Track features roughly 385 to 420 competing teams contending for \$35,000 across three specialized research awards7. Consequently, researchers submitting a rigorous, well-verified whitepaper face nearly an order-of-magnitude lower competitor density while gaining direct visibility before Google DeepMind engineers and the broader NeurIPS 2026 research community1.

| Operational Dimension | Main Prediction Competition (gemma-4-developer-agent) | Research Paper Track (gemma-4-developer-agent-paper) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Primary Deliverable** | Automated agent bundle (submission.zip with agent.yaml at root)2 | Written research report (Kaggle Writeup up to 3,000 words) plus optional arXiv PDF and public notebook1 |
| **Evaluation Mechanism** | Automated execution on \~120 hidden Python bug-fix and feature tasks7 | Human peer review by Google DeepMind and Kaggle panel across 5 equal criteria (0–5 scale)1 |
| **Final Submission Deadline** | Wednesday, December 2, 2026, at 23:59 UTC (Entry/Merger: Nov 25, 2026\)7 | Thursday, November 12, 2026, at 23:59 UTC (Nov 13, 2026, 5:29 AM IST)2 |
| **Total Prize Pool & Distribution** | **$65,000($**37,000 1st; \$18,000 2nd; \$10,000 3rd)7 | $35,000($15,000 Best Paper; \$10,000 Best Resource; \$10,000 Best Application)1 |
| **Submission Quotas** | 1 submission per day (blocked while previous run is pending); 2 Final Submissions7 | Up to 5 submissions per day; maximum of 2 Final Submissions (writeups) per team7 |
| **Tie-Breaking Protocol** | Private Leaderboard score resolution7 | First-in-time rule: the paper entered earliest into the competition wins ties1 |
| **Team & Licensing Rules** | Max 5 members; single base Gemma 4 variant (multiple LoRAs allowed); 12-hour runtime cap7 | Max 5 members; original unpublished work (arXiv preprints allowed); non-archival; Apache 2.0 license1 |

### **Strategic Positioning Across the Three Prize Archetypes**

The \$35,000 prize pool in the Paper Track is partitioned into three distinct award categories, and competition rules stipulate that a single Writeup can win only one award1. However, because each team is permitted to select up to two final submissions and submit at most two distinct writeups for judging, a research group can strategically architect either a single comprehensive manuscript or two complementary papers tailored to different award archetypes7.  
The flagship award, **Overall Best Paper (\$15,000)**, is granted to the submission achieving the highest composite score calculated as the unweighted arithmetic mean of all five rubric criteria1. Contenders for this prize must demonstrate strong empirical or theoretical originality, strict experimental controls across multiple repositories, and high external generalizability across the core competition themes of Tuning and Optimization (such as parameter-efficient LoRA fine-tuning or reinforcement learning from unit-test feedback), Code Comprehension, Tasks and Benchmarks, or Graph-based Analysis1.  
By contrast, the **Best New Resource (\$10,000)** award specifically targets contributions that build foundational infrastructure—such as a novel dataset, software library, verification harness, or developer tool—as opposed to a purely empirical study that generates experimental measurements1. Official guidance from the organizing committee, which includes Google DeepMind and Kaggle specialists Elan Markowitz, Bryan Perozzi, Benedek Rózemberczki, Glenn Cameron, Hadi Hemmati, Yuchen Li, Michael Galkin, Majid Farhadi, Ryan Holbrook, and Ashley Oldacre, highlights several high-value resource archetypes11. Competitors can construct a fine-tuning or evaluation dataset leveraging provided code embeddings, engineer a Python library that combines Gemma 4 with clustering algorithms to group code modules by underlying runtime behavior, build an interactive software dashboard to explore GitHub repositories structurally similar to a target codebase, or publish a standardized, machine-readable failure-trace dataset and deterministic replay harness for local coding agents2.  
The third category, **Best New Application (\$10,000)**, rewards creative, high-impact domain deployments that apply Gemma 4, code-graphs, or structural embeddings to novel software engineering use cases where they have not previously been utilized11. This may involve creating evaluation benchmarks for entirely new engineering tasks or applying graph representations to specialized domains outside standard web or application repositories11. A prime example cited by the organizers and validated by early competition entries is leveraging code property graphs and local Gemma 4 models to write, debug, and isolate faults in specialized hardware accelerator kernels—such as Triton, JAX Pallas, or TPU kernels—where subtle errors in matrix stride configurations or block tiling layouts cause low-level hardware crashes4.

## **Deconstructing the Five-Pillar Evaluation Rubric and the 3,000-Word Budget**

Submissions to the Gemma 4 Developer Agent Paper Track are evaluated by human reviewers across five equally weighted criteria: **Novelty**, **Quality**, **Relevance**, **Verifiability**, and **Clarity**1. Each dimension is graded on a scale from 0 (lowest) to 5 (highest), with the final score computed as the simple average of the five pillars (![][image2])1. Because individual rubric evaluations are never shared with participants and ties are broken strictly in favor of the team that entered its paper earliest into the competition, authors must self-audit every section of their manuscript against the exact definitions of these five pillars prior to submission1.  
![][image3]

### **Analytical Breakdown of the Five Judging Pillars**

A careful examination of the competition rubric reveals how each evaluation pillar interacts with the others during peer review1. **Novelty** (20% weight) evaluates whether the manuscript contributes original empirical findings, deepens scientific understanding, or uncovers critical properties of existing methods1. Crucially, originality in an academic whitepaper does not require inventing a new neural network architecture from scratch2. Demonstrating a counter-intuitive property of an existing paradigm—such as proving that stripping instructions from modular agent skills actively degrades pass rates below a zero-skill baseline (58% versus 63%), or showing that deterministic Personalized PageRank over an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) outperforms heavy neural embeddings—constitutes high-value scientific novelty4.  
**Quality** (20% weight) assesses methodological soundness and whether the proposed approach generalizes beyond the specific bounds of the competition environment1. A submission that relies on brittle regular expressions tailored solely to public sample tasks will score poorly on Quality, whereas a study that separates development tasks from held-out evaluation repositories, holds token and tool-call budgets constant across all baseline and treatment arms, and includes an explicit structural ablation will earn top marks2. **Relevance** (20% weight) measures the significance and potential impact of the research on the broader fields of software engineering and agentic learning1. Because the overarching mission of the Gemma 4 challenge is putting capable offline coding assistants onto everyday consumer hardware, papers that directly address local execution constraints—memory footprints, context compaction, latency bounds on single accelerators, and fault-tolerant tool execution—resonate strongly with this criterion1.  
**Verifiability** (20% weight) determines whether the paper includes sufficient technical detail to understand how an innovation works, how data was obtained, analyzed, and interpreted, and whether an independent reviewer can replicate the claims1. Competition hosts have emphasized that Verifiability accounts for a full fifth of the total score and that linking a clean, publicly accessible Kaggle Notebook that reproduces the paper's tables and charts is the most reliable way to secure maximum points7. Finally, **Clarity** (20% weight) evaluates structural coherence, visual presentation, and prose precision1. A competition host explicitly warned participants that purely LLM-generated writing will not score well7. Human reviewers immediately recognize the repetitive, overly abstract, and hedging cadence of unedited language-model prose; winning entries exhibit dense, human-authored technical precision where every sentence advances a formal claim, mathematical definition, or empirical observation3.

### **The Mandatory Manuscript Structure and 3,000-Word Allocation Blueprint**

The official competition guidelines enforce a strict **3,000-word maximum** for the Kaggle Writeup and mandate five core structural elements: Title and subtitle, Abstract, Introduction, Description of the research (including methods and experiments), and Related works and citations1. While authors have the option to upload an arXiv-ready LaTeX or Word PDF via the **Public Project Link** feature, the core Writeup must respect the 3,000-word ceiling rather than assuming external attachments waive the stated word limit1. The table below details how authors should partition this 3,000-word allowance to maximize rubric performance.

| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **1\. Title & Subtitle** | 15–25 words | Clarity, Relevance | Pair a memorable mechanism or system name (e.g., *TOPAZ*) in the main title with an explicit subtitle naming the base model, constraint, and empirical scope (e.g., *A Prompt-Only Gemma 4 31B Agent and the Limits of Leaderboard Scores*)3. |
| **2\. Abstract** | 175–225 words | Clarity, Novelty, Relevance | Construct a 5-sentence micro-paper: (1) The offline local-hardware bottleneck; (2) Why existing cloud-agent paradigms fail; (3) The core architectural or algorithmic contribution; (4) Exact quantitative metrics (latency, token savings, resolution rate); (5) Transferable artifacts provided3. |
| **3\. Introduction** | 350–400 words | Relevance, Novelty, Clarity | Frame local software engineering as a constrained resource-allocation problem rather than a pure coding problem3. State a falsifiable hypothesis, define the exact result that would reject that hypothesis, and specify 3–4 concrete contributions verified in the linked notebook2. |
| **4\. Related Works** | 350–400 words | Novelty, Quality | Situate the work within four literature clusters: repository-level benchmarks (SWE-bench, Jimenez et al., 2024); agentless vs. agentic workflows (Xia et al., 2024); context degradation (Liu et al., 2024; Chroma, 2025); and the Gemma 4 competition benchmark (Markowitz et al., 2026; Farhadi et al., 2026\)3. |
| **5\. Methods & Architecture** | 800–900 words | Novelty, Quality, Verifiability | Formulate the system mathematically (e.g., Code Property Graph ![][image4], Personalized PageRank damping factor ![][image5], or explicit tool-call stopping horizons)3. Include at least one structural ablation, analyze failure trajectories (e.g., timeout vs. false-stop trade-offs), and map every table to the public verification notebook2. |
| **7\. Conclusion & Citations** | 150–250 words | Clarity, Quality, Verifiability | Summarize the verified empirical findings, explicitly acknowledge boundary conditions and limitations, and provide formatted academic references alongside direct links to the public Kaggle Notebook and dataset citations1. |

## **Domain-Specific Engineering Themes for Offline Gemma 4 Coding Agents**

To score highly on **Relevance** and **Novelty**, a whitepaper must engage directly with the architectural realities of the **Gemma 4** model family and the physical constraints of local hardware execution3. Released under an Apache 2.0 license, the Gemma 4 family encompasses both dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures engineered for local workstations and edge devices, including the flagship **Gemma 4 31B Instruct** (a 30.7-billion parameter dense multimodal model supporting a 256K token context window, native function calling, and configurable deliberative thinking modes), the **Gemma 4 26B A4B** MoE variant, the mid-sized **Gemma 4 12B**, and compact edge variants (**E4B** and **E2B**)14. While Gemma 4 31B achieves strong standardized benchmark scores—including 86.2% on GPQA Diamond, 80.0% on LiveCodeBench v6, 79.7% on TAU-Bench, 69.7% on AA-LCR, 45.5% on SciCode, and 43.4% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 when its deliberative thinking mode is enabled (compared to 36.4% on Terminal-Bench Hard with thinking enabled and 30.3% in non-thinking mode)—deploying these weights inside an autonomous repository-level coding agent on consumer hardware or Kaggle's evaluation accelerators (4x NVIDIA L4 GPUs or v5e-8 TPUs) exposes severe systems bottlenecks14.  
When a local coding agent interacts with a multi-file Python repository using standard cloud-agent patterns—such as dumping raw file contents into the prompt or executing unconstrained bash exploration loops—three cascading failure modes emerge4. The first is **context window saturation and "context rot"**4. Even though Gemma 4 supports a nominal 256K context window, empirical studies (*Lost in the Middle* by Liu et al., 2024, and *Context Rot* research by Chroma, 2025\) demonstrate that language model retrieval accuracy and instruction adherence degrade substantially as input length grows, well before reaching the hard token limit5. Dumping monolithic workflow instructions or unpruned source files into the active prompt dilutes self-attention weights across hundreds of lines of irrelevant boilerplate code4.  
The second bottleneck is **quadratic prefill latency (![][image1]) and memory pressure**4. In local environments without massive distributed cloud prefill clusters, self-attention computation scales quadratically with prompt sequence length ![][image6], causing multi-turn agent trajectories to grind to a halt4. Furthermore, competitor telemetry on Kaggle's 4x L4 GPU scoring environment indicates that combining a 32K context window with high output token limits (max\_output\_tokens=8192) and active thinking traces (include\_thoughts=True) can trigger severe latency spikes or scorer-side exceptions, whereas constraining output to 4,096 tokens with include\_thoughts=False within a 5-minute, 40-call envelope completes reliably across public tasks in roughly two hours19. The third bottleneck is **unbounded exploratory loops and timeout kills**2. Small and medium local models frequently become trapped in repetitive diagnostic cycles—issuing identical search commands, re-reading the same modules, or oscillating between broken patch variants—until the task hits the wall-clock timeout2. Because a hard timeout yields zero credit and can stall or error out an entire evaluation bundle, managing the exploration-versus-exploitation budget is as critical as raw code synthesis capability3.  
Rather than feeding raw repository file dumps into the local model, high-performing architectures externalize context curation and execution governance into a four-stage deterministic pipeline2. In Stage 1 (*Static AST Graph Ingestion*), the raw codebase and issue traceback are parsed into a structural Code Property Graph without invoking heavy neural embedders4. In Stage 2 (*Causal Subgraph Pruning*), a Personalized PageRank walk seeded by traceback symbols isolates the causal execution path subgraph while pruning peripheral repository modules4. In Stage 3 (*Structural Signature Folding*), the prompt buffer separates Focal Nodes—which retain their full, editable source code—from surrounding Context Nodes, which are collapsed into compact one-line call signatures before entering the local Gemma 4 agent4. Finally, in Stage 4 (*Bounded Verification Policy*), a budget-disciplined controller enforces a hard tool-call cap, a deterministic loop detector, and targeted issue-to-test grounding to emit a verified code patch well inside hardware timeout limits2.

### **Five High-Yield Research Blueprints for Paper Track Submissions**

Drawing from official competition guidance and peer-reviewed design patterns, researchers can structure their whitepaper around one of five high-impact experimental blueprints that naturally satisfy all five rubric dimensions2. The first blueprint investigates **adaptive repository navigation under a fixed context budget**, asking whether an agent can select high-utility code-graph neighborhoods while reading significantly fewer input tokens than a fixed retrieval strategy2. A rigorous experimental design compares three arms while holding the base Gemma 4 model, evaluation tasks, and total token and tool-call budgets strictly constant: a lexical-search baseline, a fixed-radius graph-neighbor retrieval policy, and an adaptive graph expansion policy2. Authors must record resolved issues, total inspected symbols, input token consumption, and wasted navigation calls, while including an explicit ablation without graph edges to prove that structural connectivity—rather than simply retrieving a larger volume of text—drives the performance improvement2.  
A second blueprint examines **deterministic stopping and recovery policies for looping agents**, identifying the exact threshold at which halting or redirecting an agent outperforms allowing it to continue an unsuccessful exploration trajectory2. By instrumenting the harness to track repeated commands, identical traceback signatures, and oscillating patch diffs, researchers can benchmark a fixed step limit against a deterministic loop detector and a selective recovery policy2. To maintain experimental fairness, every experimental arm must receive the exact same total compute allowance (inclusive of restart work), and the evaluation must report both false stops—where a detector prematurely halts a task that was about to recover—and successful recoveries2.  
A third blueprint focuses on **issue-to-test grounding under constrained verification budgets**2. Because running an entire repository regression suite after every candidate edit rapidly exhausts local compute allowances, this study evaluates a targeted verification mechanism that links issue descriptions and modified AST symbols to a minimal subset of relevant unit tests, comparing targeted verification against broad regression policies2. By evaluating across a frozen corpus of both correct and deliberately incomplete candidate patches in a redistributable dataset, authors can rigorously quantify false patch acceptance rates, missed regressions, total verification time, and patch acceptance rates2.  
A fourth blueprint explores **smaller models with smarter verification budgets**2. Because Kaggle Staff confirmed that smaller Gemma 4 variants (such as Gemma 4 12B, 26B A4B, or E4B) are scored on the exact same hardware and 12-hour runtime limit as the heavier 31B dense model, researchers can test whether a faster, lower-parameter model paired with a larger multi-turn verification budget outperforms a 31B model restricted to a single verification pass2. Mapping the trade-off curve between parameter count, quantization precision (such as FP8 versus FP4), inference throughput, and iterative test feedback provides a highly transferable systems contribution2.  
Finally, a fifth blueprint targets the \$10,000 Best New Resource award by building **a reproducible failure-trace dataset and replay workflow** for Gemma 4 software engineering agents2. This study defines a formal, machine-readable schema capturing repository commit hashes, task identifiers, model revisions, random seeds, sequential tool calls, patch provenance, executed tests, timeouts, and hardware resource consumption2. By distinguishing between synthetic fixtures, historical replays, and fresh model runs—and supplying collection, validation, and independent replay tools—authors create an enduring benchmark asset for the open-source research community2.

## **Empirical Anatomy of High-Scoring Submissions and Experimental Rigor**

Analyzing public research papers and engineering benchmarks emerging from the Gemma 4 Paper Track and adjacent Kaggle agent whitepapers illustrates how abstract rubric criteria translate into concrete empirical evidence3. A common misconception among first-time whitepaper authors is that only a complex multi-agent fine-tuning pipeline can win2. In reality, empirical data from production agent architectures and active Gemma 4 submissions demonstrates that architectural simplicity, rigorous token economics, and honest baseline reporting are far more persuasive to peer reviewers3. The table below synthesizes the exact quantitative benchmarks from these studies to illustrate the level of empirical precision required in a top-tier manuscript.

| Study / Architecture | Core Mechanism Evaluated | Primary Empirical Metrics & Measurements | Key Scientific Finding & Rubric Alignment |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **TOPAZ** (Pokhrel, 2026 — Gemma 4 Paper Track)4 | 3-phase static AST Code Property Graph (![][image4]), Personalized PageRank (![][image5]), and Structural Signature Folding4 | CPG parse latency: **1.248 ms**; PPR pruning latency: **0.216 ms** (total **1.464 ms**, well below the **5.0 ms** target ceiling); Context volume reduction: **15.0%**4 | Externalizing graph traversal isolates root-cause faults in Triton and JAX Pallas hardware kernels without neural embedding overhead; verified via public notebook topaz\_kwe\_run4. |
| **Budget-Disciplined Prompting** (Oct 2026 — Gemma 4 Paper Track)3 | Prompt-only control policy (**3.2 KB** system prompt) on quantized Gemma 4 31B; **6 of 9** harness tools enabled; **8-minute** task budget3 | Mandatory source file edit by **12th tool call**; maximum **1 focused test** and **1 repair**; Public leaderboard baseline score: **0.13**3 | Demonstrates that an honest, modest baseline score paired with a formal resource-allocation policy, harness behavior taxonomy, and ready-to-run ablation plan constitutes a complete research contribution2. |
| **Modular Agent Skills Architecture** (Singhal et al., 2026 — Kaggle Whitepaper)5 | Refactoring monolithic system prompts into discrete, demand-loaded skill modules (SKILL.md) with DAG file-bus handoffs5 | Monolithic 50-workflow prompt: **15,000 tokens/turn** vs. Modular 50-skill library: **\~4,000** description tokens \+ **\~2,000** active body tokens (**\~6,000 tokens/turn**; **60%** reduction; **49** bodies on disk)5 | Prevents context rot by keeping inactive procedural memory on disk and shifting deterministic logic left into testable scripts5. |
| **Production Skill Invocation Telemetry** (Vercel Data cited in Kaggle Whitepaper, 2026\)5 | Multi-skill co-loading (5–15 skills) and routing evaluation across passive indexing vs. stripped instructions5 | Expected skill non-invocation rate: **56%**; Stripped skill pass rate: **58%** vs. No-skill baseline: **63%**; Passive AGENTS.md global index pass rate: **100%** vs. **53%** baseline5 | Uncovers counter-intuitive empirical anomalies: poorly constructed skills cause active harm (-5% vs. no skill), whereas passive global indexing dramatically outperforms isolated specialist routing (+47%)5. |

### **Case Study Synthesis: What Makes an Empirical Narrative Persuasive**

Examining the operational details of these three research paradigms highlights how successful authors construct their technical narratives3. In the **TOPAZ** (*Topological Agent for Zero-Bloat Code Reasoning*) submission, solo competitor Kushal Pokhrel directly addressed the physical failure modes of running Gemma 4 locally on a standard MacBook or desktop workstation: context window overflows within a few turns, attention dilution across boilerplate code, and quadratic self-attention slowdowns4. Rather than running heavy neural graph embedders or parsing intermediate bytecode, TOPAZ uses Python's built-in ast module in Phase I to map classes, functions, and call paths into a Code Property Graph ![][image7] in **1.248 ms**4. In Phase II, when an error log appears, TOPAZ extracts the traceback terms as seeds for a Personalized PageRank random walk with restarts (![][image8]) across the call graph, pruning irrelevant modules in **0.216 ms** and isolating functions along the causal execution path even when their names never appeared in the original error report4. In Phase III (*Structural Signature Folding*), TOPAZ partitions the subgraph into **Focal Nodes** (suspect functions retaining their complete, editable source code) and **Context Nodes** (surrounding callers and callees collapsed into single-line signatures formatted as \[FUNCTION\] name(args) (file.py:line) \| Calls: \[target1, target2\])4. Evaluated on hardware accelerator kernels written in **Triton** and **JAX Pallas**, TOPAZ reduced context volume by **15.0%** while maintaining exact fault isolation4. Crucially, the author maximized **Verifiability** by packaging the entire verification runner into a public Kaggle notebook (topaz\_kwe\_run) where judges can click "Run All" and verify the sub-5ms graph construction and fault isolation in seconds4.  
A second complementary paradigm is illustrated by the October 2026 Paper Track submission *Budget-Disciplined Prompting for Small Local Software Engineering Agents: A Prompt-Only Gemma 4 31B Agent and the Limits of What a Leaderboard Score Can Show*3. Recognizing that running a quantized Gemma 4 31B model on a single local accelerator transforms software engineering into a strict resource-allocation problem under an eight-minute budget, the author investigated a purely prompt-driven action policy without fine-tuning, LoRA adapters, or sub-agents3. Using a single **3.2 KB system prompt** with six of the nine harness tools enabled, the policy enforces a deterministic behavioral sequence: extract exact issue requirements, locate code via bounded reading, **edit a source file by the 12th tool call**, execute at most **one focused test and one repair**, and submit3. Although this configuration achieved a **0.13** public leaderboard score, the manuscript frames that figure appropriately as a controlled scientific baseline—contributing the formal prompt policy, an empirical analysis of the harness behaviors that shaped it, a transferable checklist for budget-limited agent prompts, and a ready-to-run ablation plan3. Practical lessons shared by competitors in the competition forums reinforce this architectural discipline: teams that budgeted for worst-case task duration rather than average duration, capped tool calls explicitly, removed sub-agents whose hand-off latency did not pay for itself, embedded stopping rules directly into the prompt, and tested slow failure paths locally avoided catastrophic timeouts and preserved valid partial submissions6.  
A third instructive paradigm comes from Kaggle's 62-page whitepaper on modular agent skills (authored by Tanvi Singhal, Gabriela Hernandez Larios, and colleagues), which demonstrates how to present token economics and ablation anomalies with mathematical clarity5. When 50 engineering workflows are concatenated into a single monolithic system prompt, an agent consumes **15,000 tokens per turn**, accelerating context rot5. Refactoring those workflows into 50 modular skills with front-loaded trigger descriptions reduces per-turn consumption to **\~4,000 description tokens plus \~2,000 active body tokens (![][image9] tokens total)** while keeping 49 inactive bodies on disk—a **60%** reduction in context overhead5. Moreover, the authors emphasize that skills must never be evaluated in isolation because production environments co-load 5 to 15 skills simultaneously, where a 5,000-word body that passes standalone tests can fail inside a populated library5. By reporting Vercel production telemetry showing a **56% non-invocation rate** for expected skills, active performance degradation when skills are stripped of instructions (**58% pass rate versus 63% with no skill**), and a **100% pass rate using a passive AGENTS.md global index** (compared to a **53% baseline**), the study provides a masterclass in reporting falsifiable, high-contrast empirical findings5.

## **Comprehensive Do's, Don'ts, and Tactical Execution Checklist**

Navigating the final stages of manuscript preparation requires strict adherence to both academic standards and the specific administrative rules of the Kaggle competition platform1. A single procedural violation—such as leaving a Writeup in draft status, pasting raw problem statements from the competition dataset, or relying on unverified LLM-generated text—can result in immediate disqualification or a severe rubric penalty regardless of the underlying engineering effort1. The table below synthesizes the essential operational mandates and prohibitions across every execution dimension.

| Operational Sub-Domain | Strategic Do (Winning Practice) | Disqualifying or Low-Scoring Don't (Trap to Avoid) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Experimental Design** | Isolate one narrow research question, establish a frozen baseline, alter a single variable at a time, and include an ablation removing the core structural mechanism2. | Alter multiple prompts, tools, and hyperparameters simultaneously, which destroys causal attribution, or ask an AI assistant to invent measurements or runs2. |
| **Benchmark Scope** | Separate development tasks from held-out evaluation repositories to prevent data leakage and demonstrate external generalizability across codebases2. | Equate a raw patch-fixing leaderboard score with paper quality; judges score scientific methodology and generalizability, not just leaderboard rank2. |
| **Prose Authorship** | Write the manuscript yourself in dense, precise academic prose and disclose any permitted AI tool usage in a dedicated attribution section7. | Submit purely LLM-generated writing; a competition host explicitly warned that purely AI-written papers will not score well with human judges7. |
| **Length & Formatting** | Keep the Kaggle Writeup strictly within the **3,000-word maximum** and include all five mandatory sections (Title/subtitle, Abstract, Intro, Methods/Experiments, Related works/citations)1. | Assume that uploading an external arXiv PDF via the Public Project Link waives the 3,000-word limit or the required section structure1. |
| **Code & Reproducibility** | Link a clean, login-free, "Run All" public Kaggle Notebook in the Project Links field to secure the full 20% **Verifiability** score1. | Require a login, paywall, or manual credential setup to view linked notebooks or external PDF manuscripts1. |
| **Dataset & Citation Hygiene** | Formally cite and link to the official competition dataset and overview (Markowitz et al., 2026; Farhadi et al., 2026\) and verify all literature references2. | Republish or copy-paste raw Kaggle problem statements or ground-truth patches directly inside the Writeup text7. |
| **Privacy & Licensing** | Audit all attached Kaggle resources before submission and ensure all shared code complies with the Open Source **Apache 2.0** license2. | Attach private Kaggle notebooks, datasets, or models containing proprietary data unless prepared for public release, as **all attached private resources automatically become public after the deadline**1. |
| **Registration & Deadlines** | Join the Paper Track competition (gemma-4-developer-agent-paper) separately, accept its rules, and click **Submit** well before **November 12, 2026, at 23:59 UTC** to capture the early-entry tie-breaker1. | Confuse the Paper Track deadline (Nov 12, 2026\) with the Main Track deadline (Dec 2, 2026), or leave a Writeup saved as an unsubmitted draft, which judges will ignore1. |
| **Team & Account Compliance** | Respect the 5-member team cap, complete any team mergers prior to the deadline, and utilize the quota of up to **2 Final Submissions** (writeups) strategically7. | Share code or data privately outside a registered team without merging, or submit from multiple Kaggle accounts, which triggers immediate disqualification7. |

### **Tactical Synthesis for Final Execution**

With the Paper Track deadline fixed at **Thursday, November 12, 2026, at 23:59 UTC**, research teams have a clear, deterministic path to maximizing their expected evaluation score2. First, authors should immediately register on the Paper Track competition page and submit an initial, complete version of their Kaggle Writeup early to lock in timestamp priority under the competition's first-entered tie-breaker rule, subsequently refining the manuscript using the five-submissions-per-day allowance1. Second, the manuscript's narrative arc should be anchored around the core physical tension of the Gemma 4 challenge: transforming a local open-weight model into a reliable, budget-disciplined software engineering agent on consumer hardware without succumbing to context rot, quadratic attention latency, or exploratory timeouts1. Third, every empirical claim in the text must be backed by a controlled multi-arm comparison and a structural ablation that a peer reviewer can verify in seconds via a linked, login-free Kaggle Notebook2. By uniting the formal methodological rigor of a NeurIPS research paper with the turnkey reproducibility of an open-source software artifact, competitors position their work to capture one of the three $10,000–$15,000 cash prizes and secure a featured showcase at the NeurIPS 2026 Google Expo1.
